label: Kimi K3.1 Pro
output:
**4 stars — Enough runtime to get out of a position safely, with a few annoying quirks**

I bought the Kestrel Bastion 1500 from Voltwise for $229 in August 2026. It’s rated at 1500VA/1000W and has pure sine wave output. I mostly wanted something that would keep my trading setup alive long enough to deal with an open position, not something to run my office for hours. After the storm on October 14, I can say it did exactly what I bought it for.

My setup is a PC, three monitors, modem, and router. While I’m trading, the Bastion’s display shows roughly **410W** for everything. During the storm, the power dropped around 2:20 p.m. while I had a **10x SOL perp long open**. The rig and Wi-Fi stayed up, and I was able to close the position cleanly in about four minutes. That alone made the purchase worth it to me. Without the backup, I would have been sitting there with a leveraged position open and no way to manage it from my desk.

I also tested the battery on purpose rather than relying completely on the box. At my usual roughly 410W load, I got **11 minutes 40 seconds** before shutting everything down myself. The box claims approximately 14 minutes at 500W. I’m not presenting my test as lab-grade, but 11:40 is a useful real-world number for anyone with a similar setup. For me, that’s enough time to close positions, save whatever I’m working on, and shut down properly. It is **not** enough to just keep trading through a long outage, so don’t buy it expecting that.

One setup detail matters a lot for traders: there are **10 outlets, but only five are battery-backed**. The other five are surge-only. Put your modem and router on the battery side too. People remember the PC and monitors, then lose internet anyway and end up with a powered-on computer showing a frozen chart. There’s also a 60W USB-C port, which is handy for keeping a phone charged.

Now for the stuff that bugs me. During the first week, the fan kicked on randomly at 3 a.m. and woke me up. It’s loud—closest comparison is a hair dryer on low. It hasn’t been a constant problem, but that was not a fun introduction to it. The outage alarm is also loud as hell. You can mute the beeping in the desktop app, but the setting reset after a firmware update, so I had to mute it again.

Speaking of the app, it looks like something from Windows XP. It’s ugly and pretty bare-bones, but the automatic shutdown function works, and that matters more to me than a modern interface. Still, for the kind of equipment people are plugging into this, the software could use some attention.

The unit itself weighs around **30 pounds**, so it’s not something you’ll want to move around constantly. I do like that the battery is swappable, although the replacement pack costs **$95**, which is worth factoring into the long-term cost.

Four stars feels right. The fan, beeping, and dated software keep it from being a five-star product, but the actual backup power worked when it mattered. If you trade from home, look at this as buying yourself a few crucial minutes to manage your risk—not as a generator. In my case, those minutes were exactly what I needed.
